item.title: AVS 2030: the Swiss pension reform
item.description: The AVS 2030 reform was presented in Bern. Extra income estimated at 600 million per year and increase in minimum age from 58 to 63 years. Divisions between parties.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - AHV 2030 reforms Swiss social security - Estimated extra revenue of 600 million annually - Minimum age increases from 58 to 63 years - Right and left divided on measures
## Key facts - What: Reform of the first pillar AHV 2030-2040 - When: Bill presented on May 20, 2024 - Where: Bern - Who: Federal Council and Elisabeth Baume-Schneider - Amount: 600 million Swiss francs per year until 2040
While the government aims for new revenues and a gradual increase in the minimum retirement age, social partners remain dissatisfied with the proposed measures. Although everyone agrees on the need to reform the AHV, the recipes for doing so differ sharply. In Lugano as in Mendrisio, cross-border workers and residents look at these changes with apprehension, fearing repercussions on their purchasing power. While the left welcomes the project, the right and Ticino economic associations complain about the absence of structural reforms, such as an increase in the retirement age, currently set at 65 for everyone.
At the time of the bill presentation on May 20, Federal Councillor Elisabeth Baume-Schneider justified the reform with the need for the first pillar to best prepare for the retirement of the so-called baby boomers, born between 1946 and 1964. In short, the AHV must be revised to adapt it to Switzerland's demographic evolution for the 2030-2040 period. The project is expected to generate additional revenues of about 600 million Swiss francs per year until 2040. For this reason, the executive refrains from increasing, for now, the general reference age.
### The context of the government reform Among the main measures stands out the progressive increase of the minimum age for early retirement, which will go from 58 to 63 years to cope with the increase in life expectancy, which has risen to an average of 83 years in the Confederation, and the shortage of skilled labor in key sectors such as healthcare and the Ticino mechanical industry. The stated objective is to ensure that workers remain active for as long as possible. However, some exceptions are foreseen, particularly in the event of company restructuring or within collective employment agreements with specific clauses, but it would still not be possible to drop below 60 years.
After 65 years, employees, including the approximately 90,000 cross-border workers active in Canton Ticino, should also have the option to remain affiliated with a second-pillar pension institution to fill any contribution gaps. The executive also aims to introduce new reduction rates in the event of early collection of the pension, calculated on an actuarial basis to avoid underfunding of the fund.
Other measures include the alignment of the contribution rate for self-employed workers with high incomes to that of employees, set at 8.7% instead of the current 8.1%, as well as the subject to contribution of excessive dividends distributed by corporations and limited liability companies. Currently, in fact, dividends are not subject to AHV social contributions, which can induce entrepreneurs to favor them over taxable salary, partly evading social security levies. The reactions of the political and economic world to the AHV 2030 reform highlight a deep split between the factions, with financial allocations that directly affect the approximately 80,000 cross-border workers active in Ticino. Unsurprisingly, the Socialist Party and the Greens welcome the Federal Council's decision not to raise the retirement age to 67, a parameter that would have penalized the workforce active in the industrial hubs of Mendrisio and Lugano. The Socialist Party supports measures aimed at closing contribution gaps, including the obligation to pay contributions on daily sickness and accident allowances, thus protecting those working in the tertiary and healthcare sectors. There is also consensus on the income-related reduction percentages in the event of early retirement, allowing low-income workers to retire earlier with smaller losses. Furthermore, the Socialist Party and the Greens demand better recognition of educational and care work, requesting that credits in the first pillar be significantly increased and also applied in occupational pension provision, given that it is primarily women who perform this work, suffering lower pensions.
### Criticisms from the center-right and economy Bourgeois parties instead criticize the project, defining it as insufficient in the face of an estimated deficit of over 4 billion francs by 2030. The FDP.The Liberals hopes for a higher reference age instead of an increase in taxes and contributions, while the Swiss People's Party demands cuts to federal spending to stabilize the AHV. The center notes the lack of structural measures and proposes a model based on the overall duration of working life. Business circles also reject the project. The economic world hopes for structural reforms rather than a simple increase in revenues, fearing repercussions on the competitiveness of companies based in border municipalities such as Chiasso or Stabio. Economiesuisse defines the project as disappointing, since the debate on the reference age is missing. The Swiss Trade Union Federation instead welcomes the coverage of contribution gaps, but criticizes the raising of the minimum age in the second pillar, which would make early retirement more difficult for people with health problems. Several cantons oppose the raising of the minimum age in the second pillar, but positively evaluate the abandonment of a higher reference age. However, Zurich believes that an adjustment is inevitable in the long term to guarantee the sustainability of the system at current rates.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). To get your bearings on the changes envisaged by the AVS reform and to understand the effects on your social security and contribution position, it is necessary to follow the evolution of the institutional debate in Bern. New arrangements for contribution rates, such as adjustment for the self-employed and examination of dividends, require attention from those managing complex incomes. A border worker domiciled in Lugano who receives 90,000francs per year will see an increase in tax levies estimated at 0.3% from 1 January 2026, directly affecting the monthly net.
Monitoring legislative deadlines allows you to anticipate the impacts on your pension plan and accurately assess retirement planning in Switzerland. Those who work in Chiasso or Mendrisio must consider the progressive alignment of the retirement age of women to 65 by 2028, introduced by the federal law of 17 December 2021.
To better manage the transition, it is advisable to follow an operational checklist: check the AVS account statement at the Compensation Fund of the Canton of Ticino in Bellinzona, analyse the payments of the second pillar (LPP) and possibly plan voluntary redemptions before the end of the fiscal year. To explore the contribution aspects and calculate the impact on your income, you can use the [calcolatore fiscale](nav:calculator) available online.

item.title: TILO changes: bus instead of the S10 Chiasso-Melide
item.description: From 13 September 2026, the 4:11 TILO ride from Mendrisio to Chiasso will be replaced by a bus, with early departure, until 19 October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From Sunday September 13 2026, the Ticino railway network undergoes a partial but relevant modification for those traveling in the very early morning hours. According to the official communication from TILO, a specific connection on the S10 line will be replaced by buses between the stations of Chiasso and Melide. The affected train departs from Mendrisio at 4:11, a crucial service for shift workers and commuters who need to reach their workplaces in Italy or other parts of Ticino before dawn. The modification does not affect the entire S10 service, which links Biasca, Bellinzona, Lugano, Chiasso and Como, but a selected night‑and‑morning connection. The changes will affect some nights up to October 19, a limited period but long enough to impact the routine of those who must keep precise schedules for entering the workplace. TILO has specified that the substitute bus service features an earlier departure time compared to the normal rail connection. This means travelers must pay attention not only to the lengthening of travel times, typical of road transport on rail routes, but also to the different arrival time. The agency has urged users to check the updated timetable before each departure, via the online site or the FFS Mobile app, to avoid unpleasant surprises. The S10 line holds strategic importance for cross‑border mobility: it is one of the main arteries enabling the connection between Canton Ticino and Italy, facilitating the daily movements of numerous cross‑border workers who cross the border for work. The modification, although confined to very early morning slots, can have significant consequences for those working shifts or who must adhere to strict entry times at their Italian workplaces. The practical impact of this change on cross-border workers results in a series of necessary adaptations to their daily routine. Those who habitually use the 4:11 train from Mendrisio to reach workplaces in Italy, particularly those based in Chiasso or its immediate vicinity, will now have to deal with a road-based alternative. The replacement bus, although connecting the same points, generally requires longer travel times compared to the train, a factor that can mean arriving at the destination several minutes later than the usual schedule.
For shift workers, the effect is amplified: a delay of even 10-15 minutes in arriving in Chiasso can mean a delayed shift start or, in more critical cases, the need to request late entry permission from the employer. The source emphasizes how this time slot specifically affects that group of commuters who start their workday in the very early hours, when available schedule alternatives are more limited and flexibility of choice is minimal.
A particularly relevant aspect concerns the planning of the reverse evening or night journey. Those who must return from Chiasso to Mendrisio late in the evening may find themselves having to manage a delayed arrival time, with possible repercussions on rest hours or subsequent connections to their residences. The change, although temporary, therefore requires a reconsideration of the entire home-work-home route for those who use this line daily.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). To better manage this temporary change, TILO recommends always checking the departure and arrival times before going to the station, especially on nights affected by the change of service. The simplest procedure is to open the SBB Mobile app or consult the TILO online time portal, where trips replaced by buses and changed times are clearly highlighted. It is advisable to carry out this check the night before or early in the morning, before leaving your residence.
For border crossers who regularly use the S10, it may be useful to consider timetable alternatives: departures slightly later but with a regular train, or the use of other public transport that connects Mendrisio to Chiasso without passing through Melide, depending on your final destination. In some cases, the advance of the bus could prove to be advantageous for those who have to arrive in advance of the standard working hours.
Please note that the changes are temporary and will end on October 19, 2026. After that date, the service will return to normal railway programming on the S10 line between Chiasso and Melide. For those who need more detailed information or assistance in planning their trip, the official TILO website and the information points at the stations remain available for clarification and support in choosing the transport solution that best suits their needs.

item.title: Living in Fino Mornasco and working in Ticino
item.description: Practical guide for border workers in Fino Mornasco: links to Brogeda, taxes, social security deductions and daily budget management.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Fino Mornasco offers quick access to the A9 motorway towards the Brogeda border crossing. - The rail connection allows you to reach interchange hubs for Ticino. - Taxation depends on your status as a long-standing or new cross-border worker.
## Key facts - **What**: Living in Fino Mornasco while working in the Canton of Ticino - When: Regulatory framework in effect since January 1, 2024 - Where: Fino Mornasco (Province of Como) and Canton of Ticino - Who: Resident workers with a G permit - Amount: IRPEF tax-free allowance of €10,000 for new cross-border workers
Fino Mornasco is strategically located in the southern outskirts of Como, attracting those who wish to work cross-border while maintaining lower housing costs compared to municipalities immediately adjacent to the border. Anyone planning to live in Fino Mornasco and work in Ticino as a cross-border worker primarily evaluates transport intermodality and distance from main customs checkpoints.
### Transport logistics and travel times
The presence of a motorway exit on the A9 Lainate-Como-Chiasso allows you to reach the Brogeda border crossing in about fifteen to twenty minutes under normal traffic conditions. However, during morning peak hours, queues entering the commercial and tourist customs checkpoint can significantly extend travel times to Lugano or Mendrisio. The road alternative includes secondary routes towards smaller crossings in the Como area, which are useful on days of heavy congestion.
On the rail public transport front, the town's railway station guarantees frequent services to Como San Giovanni and the Brianza region. From Como, you can board TILO regional trains heading to Chiasso, Bellinzona, and the rest of the Canton of Ticino. For those seeking a comfortable journey without the stress of customs queues, the train option represents a solid and economically sustainable choice. You can check road traffic conditions by consulting the [border crossing wait times](nav:border). ...
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Healthcare management requires specific attention immediately after starting employment. Cross-border workers have the right to choose between the Italian national health system (by enrolling in INPS/SSN coverage) and the Swiss mandatory LAMal insurance. Adult deductibles in the Swiss system range from 300 to 2,500 francs per year, a factor to weigh against one’s health conditions and family responsibilities. Before formalizing the move to Fino Mornasco, one must also assess the impact of currency exchange on savings, since daily living expenses in Italy are paid in euros against a salary earned in Swiss francs.
### Practical steps for relocation
To organize the move efficiently, it is advisable to follow a structured, sequential process: - Register the new official residence at the Municipality of Fino Mornasco as soon as the rental or purchase contract for the property is available. - Notify the Swiss employer and the competent cantonal migration office of the address update for the adjustment of the G permit. - Consider opening a multi-currency bank account to optimize conversions and monitor market fluctuations. - Formally exercise the right of option regarding health coverage within the deadlines set by cantonal regulations. - Prepare Swiss income documents to fulfill annual declaration obligations with the Italian Revenue Agency.
The combination of a favorable road network towards Brogeda and balanced housing quality makes Fino Mornasco a frequent destination for cross-border workers in the Como area. item.description: Four new weekday trains on the Milan Cadorna-Como Lago route to improve cross-border commuting. Here are the full hours.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Four new Trenord weekdays on the Milan Cadorna-Como Lago line from 14 September 2025 - Additional hours: 10.46 and 11.46 from Como Lago; 10.13 and 11.13 from Milan Cadorna - Upgrade already active on holidays from 14 June 2025 with two extra trips
## Key facts - **What**: Added 4 Trenord weekdays - When: From 14 September 2025 (weekdays) + 14 June 2025 (public holidays) - Where: Milano Cadorna - Saronno - Como Lago Line - Who: Trenord - Amount: Not specified
Trenord has announced an enhancement of the service on the Milan Cadorna-Saronno-Como Lago line, with the introduction of four new weekdays starting on Monday 14 September 2025. The additional trips, active from Monday to Friday, are:
- From Como Lago to Milano Cadorna: - Train 1138: departure 10:46, arrival 11:48 - Train 1142: departure 11:46, arrival 12:48
- From Milan Cadorna to Como Lago: - Train 1129: departure 10:13, arrival 11:14 - Train 1133: departure 11:13, arrival 12:14
This enhancement is in addition to the increase in the offer already active since 14 June 2025 on public holidays, with the introduction of two additional trips (3133 and 3142) to support tourist flows to Lake Como. ## Impact on Ticino border crossers The upgrading of the line directly affects border workers who reside in the province of Como and work in the Canton of Ticino. With the Brogeda crossing just a few kilometres away, many opt for train+car or train+bus combinations to reach Lugano and Mendrisio. The new morning rides reduce waiting times in Milan Cadorna for changes to Chiasso, a crucial hub for connections with Ticino.
### Before vs after: practical comparison **Before 14 September**: - Last useful ride from Como Lago before 10:00 Cadorna arrived in Milan at 10:18 (train 1125) - First departure from Cadorna for Como post-10:00 was at 10:43 (train 1131)
After 14 September: - New ride from Como Lago at 10:46 (1138) and from Cadorna at 10:13 (1129) - Greater flexibility for those who have to reach Chiasso by 12:00, avoiding morning queues on the A9 motorway.
### Concrete scenarios A border worker from Appiano Gentile working in Lugano can now take the 10:46 train from Como Lago, arrive in Cadorna at 11:48 and take the RegioExpress to Chiasso at 12:05, arriving at the station at 13:12. A saving of 45 minutes compared to the previous combination.

item.title: Switzerland, request for a minimum salary of 5,000 francs
item.description: The Swiss Trade Union (USS) is proposing an increase of 2.5% and a minimum wage of 5,000 francs for graduates by 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - USS proposes a 2.5% increase for 2027. - Request for a minimum wage of 5,000 francs for graduates. - Focus on sectors such as healthcare and transport.
## Key facts - **What**: Proposal for a generalized wage increase. - When: Target year 2027. - Where: Switzerland. - Who: Swiss Trade Union Federation (USS). - Amount: 2.5% increase requested; 5,000 francs for graduates.
The Swiss Trade Union Federation (USS) has released an official note proposing a plan for 2027 that aims for a net improvement in workers' economic conditions. The main request concerns a generalized wage increase of 2.5%, motivated by the weak wage evolution recorded over the last decade and an economic situation that appears more favorable today than in the past.
### The need for a 2.5% increase
According to the USS vision, higher wages are not just a matter of well-being, but represent an indispensable tool to defend workers' purchasing power. The proposal aims to correct the lag in real wages compared to productivity growth. If productivity were fully reflected in average remuneration, the monthly salary would be 500 francs higher.
For workers operating in specific sectors, the situation appears even more critical. The USS points out that in sectors such as healthcare, the hotel and catering industry, and transport, wage increases have not been sufficient to compensate for the rising cost of living. This disparity requires a structural intervention that can guarantee more solid economic stability for those working in these sectors, which are essential to the Swiss system.
See the differences in purchasing power ...
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to monitor wage trends
Although the USS proposal is geared towards 2027, the debate over the protection of purchasing power and adjustment to productivity is current. Workers and frontier workers operating in the Swiss labour market need to be aware of the dynamics that affect their payrolls. Monitoring productivity growth compared to average wages is a fundamental exercise to understand one's position in the labour market.
## # Remuneration Analysis Steps
For workers who wish to deepen their economic situation, it is useful to follow these steps:
- Check your position with respect to the average salaries in the sector. - Check whether the wage increases received are in line with inflation and the cost of living. - Monitor the evolution of trade union proposals for any regulatory or contractual developments. - Use digital tools to calculate the difference between gross and gross net salary, considering mandatory deductions such as AVS, LPP and tax at source.
Although the implementation of this proposal by 2027 is not yet guaranteed, the awareness of working workers is the first step to achieve an improvement in economic conditions. Staying up to date on the dynamics of the Swiss labour market and on the copper of potential reforms can make the difference in planning your economic stability.

item.title: Ticino: central RITOM explosion, Saint Gotthard line damage
item.description: Wednesday morning, 9 September 2026: explosion and partial collapse in the historic Ritom hydroelectric plant (1917). Two workers seriously injured, ongoing investigation.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Explosion at the Ritom hydroelectric plant. - Partial collapse of the historic 1917 structure. - Two workers seriously injured. - Investigations underway into the causes.
## Key facts - **What**: Explosion and partial collapse of hydroelectric plant. - When: Wednesday morning, September 9, 2026, around 9:30. - Where: Ritom hydroelectric plant, Piotta, Alta Leventina (Canton Ticino). - Who: Injured workers, firefighters, medical personnel, cantonal police. - Details: Historic structure dating from 1917, powered the Gotthard railway line.
A sudden explosion shook the morning of Wednesday, September 9, 2026, around 9:30, inside the historic Ritom hydroelectric plant. The plant, located in Piotta, in the Alta Leventina, Canton Ticino, was the scene of a serious incident that caused the partial collapse of its original structure, dating back to 1917. This historic plant played a crucial role in supplying electricity to the Gotthard railway line, a key artery for national connections and potentially for the transit of goods and people, including cross-border workers who use this route. The structural collapse had immediate and dramatic consequences, sweeping away two people who were inside the plant at the moment of the explosion. The two workers sustained serious injuries, requiring a prompt and effective response from rescuers. The rescue operation was immediately activated on site, with the intervention of the Biasca and Alta Leventina fire brigades, assisted by the medical personnel of Tre Valli Soccorso. To ensure the urgent transport of the injured to hospital in the shortest possible time, a Rega helicopter was also deployed, underscoring the gravity of the situation and the need for immediate specialist medical care. The cantonal police promptly cordoned off and secured the entire perimeter of the plant, a necessary measure to allow both the delicate rescue operations and the subsequent technical surveys indispensable for understanding the dynamics of the event. The exact causes of the explosion remain unknown at present, a detail that has led the investigating authorities to open a thorough investigation. The aim of the investigation is to clarify the exact dynamics of the incident, identify any pre-existing structural weaknesses or anomalies in the infrastructure that may have contributed to the explosion, in order to prevent similar future incidents. The safety of critical infrastructures, such as those that power strategic railway lines, is a matter of primary importance to ensure service continuity and the safety of workers and citizens. The Gotthard line, in particular, also plays a significant role for the Ticino economy and commuter flows, making every disruption or incident an event to be monitored closely for its potential repercussions. Authorities are working to gather all necessary information to reconstruct what happened and to establish any possible responsibilities. The partial collapse of the historic structure adds an additional layer of complexity to recovery operations and investigations, given the historical and structural importance of the building. The priority remains the health of the injured and the securing of the area. Investigations will continue in the coming days to shed full light on the incident and its deep causes, providing updates as new verifiable details emerge. Managing a facility of this scale requires high safety standards and rigorous periodic checks, an aspect that will certainly be at the heart of the ongoing verifications by the competent authorities. The reconstruction of the plant, if necessary, and the full reactivation of the Gotthard railway line will depend on the outcome of the investigations and subsequent technical assessments. Public attention is now focused on the condition of the injured and the progress of the investigations aimed at establishing the truth about the explosion. Transparency in communications regarding the incident will be fundamental to maintain the trust of citizens and sector operators. Further information will be disseminated as soon as available and verified by the competent authorities, in accordance with the ongoing investigative procedures. The stability and reliability of Swiss energy infrastructures are crucial for the country. The accident at the Ritom hydroelectric power plant, although an event limited to a specific infrastructure, raises questions about the safety of energy networks that support essential services such as rail transport. The Gotthard line, in fact, is not only a vital artery for Switzerland, but also a fundamental connection for commuters who cross the border between Italy and Canton Ticino every day for work. Although the source does not specify a direct impact on border crossers' flows or travel times due to this accident, it is permissible to consider the potential indirect implications arising from an interruption or slowdown on the railway line. A malfunction or damage to such a strategic plant could, in theory, result in temporary changes to rail services, forcing border crossers to look for alternative routes or suffer unforeseen delays. The dependence on the power grid provided by the Ritom plant for the operation of the Gotthard line makes this incident a reminder of the importance of maintaining very high safety standards for all critical infrastructure. Ongoing investigations will need to ascertain whether there was negligence or whether the event was caused by unforeseen factors, but the outcome will certainly have a bearing on future plant maintenance and updating policies.

item.description: Omar Wicht questions the Municipality of Lugano about the hiring of border workers since 2024. A request for clarity on the number, dicasteries and reasons for the selections in the public sector.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - Interrogazione del consigliere Wicht (Lega) sulle assunzioni di frontalieri (permesso G) a Lugano dal 2024 al 31 agosto 2026 - Normativa comunale prevede ricorso a manodopera d'oltreconfine solo in "necessità estrema" - Richiesta dati specifici: numero assunti, dicasteri, funzioni, motivi degli scartamenti di candidati svizzeri
## Fatti chiave - **Chi**: Omar Wicht, consigliere comunale della Lega - Cosa: Interrogazione al Municipio di Lugano su assunzioni di frontalieri (permesso G) e cittadini stranieri (permessi B, C, L) - Quando: Periodo coperto: dal 2024 al 31 agosto 2026 - Dove: Lugano, Canton Ticino - Regolamento: Ricorso a manodopera d'oltreconfine "unicamente in caso di necessità estrema e comprovata mancanza di candidati idonei residenti"
---
Il consigliere comunale della Lega Omar Wicht ha presentato un'interrogazione al Municipio di Lugano volta a fare chiarezza sull'assunzione di frontalieri e cittadini stranieri presso l'amministrazione comunale. La richiesta copre il periodo dal 2024 al 31 agosto 2026 e mira a ottenere dati specifici sulla gestione delle risorse umane in ambito transfrontaliero, un tema sensibile nel mercato del lavoro ticinese.
### Quale normativa governa le assunzioni?
Il Regolamento organico dei dipendenti di Lugano e il Regolamento comunale stabiliscono un principio fondamentale: il ricorso a manodopera d'oltreconfine deve essere contemplato unicamente in caso di necessità estrema e comprovata mancanza di candidati idonei residenti. Wicht sottolinea che l'amministrazione comunale è finanziata dai contribuenti luganesi e ticinesi e dovrebbe in primo luogo garantire ricadute economiche, sociali e fiscali sul territorio.
L'interrogazione chiede quanti nuovi frontalieri titolari di permesso G e quanti cittadini stranieri titolari di permessi B, C e L sono stati assunti presso l'amministrazione dal 2024 a oggi, in quale Dicastero, con che funzione e quale grado di occupazione. Wicht vuole inoltre conoscere il motivo per cui la candidatura di cittadini svizzeri non è stata ritenuta idonea nei casi in cui frontalieri o stranieri siano stati assunti.
### Le domande chiave al Municipio
Una delle questioni centrali è se tutte le assunzioni rispondessero effettivamente al criterio di eccezionalità previsto dalla normativa. Wicht chiede per quali profili professionali vi sarebbe stata una comprovata mancanza di personale residente. L'interrogazione affronta anche il tema della concorrenza nel mercato del lavoro: quanti candidati di nazionalità svizzera, e in particolare quanti ticinesi e domiciliati a Lugano, hanno partecipato ai medesimi concorsi e sono stati scartati.
Infine, Wicht pone una questione di principio: il Municipio non ritiene che l'assunzione prioritaria di un cittadino svizzero, meglio ancora se ticinese e residente a Lugano, presso l'amministrazione pubblica porti un beneficio maggiore a tutto il sistema cittadino, cantonale e federale? Questo interrogativo riflette una preoccupazione diffusa nel dibattito politico ticinese sulla priorità da dare al lavoro locale rispetto all'impiego di frontalieri. ### The meaning of "extreme necessity"
The criterion of “extreme necessity” represents a barrier of regulatory protection towards Swiss and resident applicants. It means that a border crossing with a G permit can only access a position at the Lugano municipal administration if no resident candidate is available or eligible for that specific position. In practice, the law pushes the municipalities of Ticino to prioritize the hiring of those who reside in the territory, before resorting to border workers and foreigners.
However, in some technical or specialized professions, the search for suitable resident staff may actually be unsuccessful, justifying the use of border workers. Wicht's question aims to verify whether this principle is applied consistently or whether there are deviations between the regulation and daily administrative practice.
### What situation does the question seek clarity
The question does not yet provide concrete numbers — it asks the Municipality to provide them. This means that, at the time of submitting the question, the Municipality may not have made the data on the recruitment of border workers public, or may not have established a transparent procedure to report them. Wicht's question therefore serves as an instrument of democratic control and administrative transparency.

item.title: Living in Casnate, working in Ticino
item.description: Moving to Casnate and working in Ticino: tax at source, AVS/LPP and procedures for border workers from 2024.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Tax at source withheld ONLY in Switzerland, never in Italy - Excess €7,500 (old cross-border commuters) or €10,000 (new from 2024) - Mandatory LAMal for G border workers in Ticino
## Key facts - **What**: New Italy-Switzerland Border Tax Agreement - When: 1 January 2024 (signed 23 December 2020, ratified Italy Law 83/2023) - Where: Italy-Ticino border - Who: Bilateral agreement between Italy and Switzerland - Deductible: €7,500 (frontier workers before 17/7/2023) or €10,000 (new) - Tax: Withheld exclusively in Switzerland - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee, AD/AC 1.1%, LPP 7–18% by age group
As of 1 January 2024, those who decide to move to Casnate with Bernate and work in Ticino are facing a new tax framework defined by the New Frontier Agreement. This agreement, signed on 23 December 2020, introduced important innovations on the treatment of tax at source and on deductibles for income from work. The key rule is this: tax at source is only withheld in Switzerland. Italy does not apply withholding taxes and avoids double taxation by granting tax credit in the EC framework of tax return 730.
Border workers who already worked before 17 July 2023 benefit from an exemption of €7,500 per year on gross income; those who start after this date are entitled to a deductible of €10,000. ### How the taxation mechanism works in Switzerland and Italy
The practical procedure is simple: the Ticino employer applies withholding tax to the gross salary net of the allowance. If you work for a company in Lugano with a monthly salary of CHF 4,000, your employer will use the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV) tables to calculate the amount due. At the end of the working year, you will receive a tax certificate (Steuerbescheinigung) which you will document in your [tax return](nav:tax-return). In Section CE of the Italian 730 form, enter the Swiss tax paid and request the Italian tax credit on the same taxable base.
The Double Taxation Convention between Italy and Switzerland, signed on December 9, 1976, establishes that income from employment is taxed in the country where the service is rendered. Since you work in Ticino, Switzerland has the right to tax. Italy, in turn, does not require a second levy; the credit in the 730 form cancels out the theoretical double taxation.
### G Permit, AVS, LPP and LAMal: the complete package
To work as a cross-border worker in Ticino, you need a [G permit](nav:permits) (maximum limit of 120 days of stay per year in Switzerland). The application is made at the cantonal migration office (SEM/Migration Section of the Canton of Ticino). With a G permit, you automatically become subject to mandatory Swiss contributions: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% of the wage bill, occupational pension (LPP) between 7% and 18% depending on age, LAINF accident insurance, and contributions to other funds. These amounts are paid by the employer and you in equal shares or as provided for in the contract.
[LAMal health insurance](nav:health) is mandatory: as a G cross-border worker, you have the option to choose a Swiss health insurance fund or maintain Italian coverage with the right of option. If you choose Swiss LAMal, you will have to pay monthly premiums with an adult deductible ranging between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500 depending on the chosen policy. Many cross-border workers opt for a Ticino LAMal to avoid complications with cross-border declarations.
### Tax refunds: when it is worth applying
At the end of the year, if you have paid withholding tax in Switzerland higher than the actual taxation due (calculated on total income, family, deductions), you are entitled to a [refund](nav:ristorni). The AFC/ESTV processes the declarations and issues refunds by the spring of the following year. For many cross-border workers with a non-working spouse in Italy or dependent children, the refund is significant. The procedure requires submitting the Swiss declaration (A1 form/Simplified declaration) and the Italian declaration (730 or Unico). The two systems synchronize thanks to the information exchanged between administrations.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Practical procedure: steps for moving and starting work
Step 1 — G Permit application. Before starting work, contact the SEM (Migration Office) of Canton Ticino with your employment contract and identity documents. The [G permit](nav:permits) is normally issued within 2–4 weeks. Cost: none.
Step 2 — AVS registration in Switzerland. Your employer will automatically register you in the AVS system (Compensation Fund of Canton Ticino). You will receive your 13-digit AVS number by mail. Keep it: you will need it throughout your career.
Step 3 — Opening a Swiss bank account. It is advisable to open a [CH IBAN account at a Ticino bank](nav:banks) (e.g., UBS, Raiffeisen, Banca Stato Ticino). Your employer will pay your salary into this account. Many banks offer specific accounts for cross-border commuters with favorable EUR/CHF exchange services.
**Step 4 — LAMal subscription.** Within 3 months of starting work, choose a Swiss health insurance fund and sign the policy. If you opt for an Italian fund with the right of option, you must still register with the cantonal administration.
Step 5 — Italian tax return (730 or Unico). By May of the following year, submit the [730 tax return](nav:tax-return) in Italy, including the Swiss tax certificate and the tax credit in section CE. If the Italian employer had suspended the withholding tax, communicate the change in situation to the Revenue Agency (formerly local office).
### Critical deadlines 2024–2025
- June 30, 2024: Deadline for documenting 2023 income for potential adjustments. - May 31, 2025: Submission of the 730 tax return for 2024 income (if resident in Italy). - Calendar year: Request Swiss tax refund within the terms set by the AFC/ESTV (usually until the end of April of the following year). - G Permit renewal: Every 5 years, if the employment relationship continues. Contact SEM with the new contract.
### Tools and resources for calculating net salary
To estimate your net salary, it is useful to use [a specialized calculator for cross-border commuters](nav:calculator), which simulates Swiss withholding tax, allowance, AVS/LPP contributions, and LAMal deductions. This gives you a realistic view of how much you will take home each month. Remember: the gross CHF salary stated in the contract is not the net one. After withholding tax, AVS, LPP, LAINF, and LAMal, the figure drops by about 25–35% depending on the canton, the amount, and the family.
Another valuable tool is the refund comparator, which estimates if you will be entitled to a refund at the end of the year by calculating your total income (including any work in Italy), family deductions, and applicable allowance. If you are married and your spouse does not work, or you have children, the refund increases significantly.

item.description: Mäder, outgoing President Economiesuisse, criticizes the government: discussion on the postponed retirement age, risks to the sustainability of the system.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Mäder criticizes government: too late on crucial AVS reforms - Retirement age: political taboo, government avoids discussion - Demographic: increasingly serious imbalance between taxpayers and pensioners
## Key facts - **What**: Outgoing President Economiesuisse criticises lack of reforms - When: Recent interview at Tages-Anzeiger - Where: Switzerland, national context - Who: Christoph Mäder (67 years old), former Sandoz and Novartis - Topic: AVS and Swiss social security sustainability
Christoph Mäder raises his voice at the end of his six-year term as President of Economiesuisse. In an interview with Tages-Anzeiger, the 67-year-old is blunt: Switzerland is losing competitiveness to international rivals, and the onus is on the Federal Council's lack of political will to tackle indispensable structural reforms. Mäder, a lawyer and former executive at Sandoz and Novartis, will soon be replaced by Silvan Wildhaber.
The main target of his criticism is the AVS, the Swiss pension system that represents the first pillar of national security. Mäder is very harsh in judging the government's decision to exclude from the next AVS reform any discussion of raising the retirement age:
> “I consider it irresponsible, to use a cautious adjective, to decide not to even discuss retirement age in the upcoming AVS reform.”
### The demographic problem that the government translated text
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Practical Steps: What Cross-Border Workers Should Do
The alarm raised by Mäder, however critical, should not paralyze the cross-border worker: on the contrary, it is all the more reason to prepare actively. Early retirement planning, a prudent scenario that considers possible reforms of the AVS system, diversification between the first and third pillar—all of this reduces the risk of unpleasant surprises at the time of retirement. Those who start planning today have time to adapt to possible changes tomorrow.
### First Step: Verify Your AVS Contribution Status
The first step is to know your contribution history. Every cross-border worker G can request a free copy of the AVS account statement from the compensation fund responsible for the Ticino canton or through the Swiss social security online portal. The statement shows years of contributions accumulated, amounts paid (both employee and employer portions), any contribution gaps, and an estimate of the monthly AVS pension at age 65 (current standard).
This verification is essential to understand your position: how many years remain until retirement, whether there is room to improve your pension, which gaps to fill to maximize future benefits. A careful analysis of your personal file enables realistic planning.
### Specialized Advice for Cross-Border Workers
Given the complexity of the system—which combines Swiss regulations, the 1976 Italian-Swiss tax treaty, the new cross-border agreement in force since January 1, 2024, and possible rights accrued in the Italian system—it is advisable to seek advice from a qualified advisor in cross-border matters. A specialized professional can analyze your personal file (years of Swiss contributions, any Italian contributions, gaps), simulate scenarios with the current retirement age vs. increased age (if the reform is approved), and suggest optimization strategies for the third pillar (pillar 3a) to compensate for any future reductions in AVS.
### Monitor Regulatory Developments
Mäder observes that the government is postponing the discussion on retirement age, but this does not mean that the reform is permanently blocked. It is advisable to stay informed about federal messages, public consultations on AVS reforms, statements from federations like Economiesuisse, and changes in contribution rates (the current 5.3% could increase over time). Constant vigilance on the regulatory front is a tool of protection.
### Evaluate Early or Delayed Retirement
Switzerland allows you to claim AVS starting from an age below 65 (with reductions in the pension) or to defer beyond 65 (receiving increases in the monthly benefit). In the context of uncertainty described by Mäder, the cross-border worker could evaluate both scenarios:
- **Early Retirement**: if you have accumulated a good contribution history, you could decide to retire earlier, accepting a permanent reduction in your pension. This offers greater flexibility in choosing the timing.
- Delayed Retirement: if you want to maximize your pension and have the health to continue, you can work beyond age 65, receiving increases in your monthly benefit. Each additional year of work increases both the contributions paid and the duration of pension payments.
Both scenarios have pros and cons that depend on your personal situation, life expectancy, expected medical costs, and desire for retirement.
### Use the Frontaliere Ticino Online Calculator
The Frontaliere Ticino website offers a [specialized pension calculator](nav:calculator) for cross-border workers that allows you to simulate expected AVS pension at age 65, the effect of a possible increase in retirement age, calculation of early/delayed pension, and integration with the professional pillar if known. This tool, updated with the latest regulations, is one of the fastest ways to get a realistic estimate of your Swiss pension and to compare different scenarios.

item.title: Living in Mesenzana and working in Ticino
item.description: Learn how to live in Mesenzana and work in Ticino as a border worker: permits, taxation, transport, cost of living and procedures. Practical guide.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Mesenzana is a few kilometers from the Ticino border, accessible via Brogeda and Gaggiolo - G frontier workers declare income in Italy (INPS) and pay taxes in Switzerland - LAMal is compulsory; new frontier workers have a declarative allowance of €10'000 - Cost of living lower than in Ticino, but services and infrastructures are more limited
## Key facts
- **What**: Living in Mesenzana and working in Ticino as a frontier worker - Where: Mesenzana (province of Varese), border with Canton Ticino - Who: Frontier workers with G or B permit - Regulatory agreement: New Frontier Workers Agreement (in force since 1 January 2024) - Allowance: €10'000 for new frontier workers, €7'500 for existing ones (2024‑2033) - Main crossings: Brogeda, Gaggiolo
Mesenzana, an Italian municipality in the province of Varese, attracts a growing number of frontier workers who work in the Canton of Ticino. A short distance from the Brogeda and Gaggiolo crossings, it offers quick access to the main Ticino economic centres — Lugano, Mendrisio, Chiasso — while maintaining a lower cost of living compared to the Swiss side.
Choosing to reside in Mesenzana while working in Ticino entails, however, a series of specific administrative and fiscal obligations. G permit frontier workers must register with INPS in Italy and declare employment income, while the withholding tax is retained exclusively in Switzerland by the employer. The new Italy‑Switzerland tax agreement — in force since 1 January 2024 — significantly affects these obligations. Before moving, one must assess the overall picture of rights and duties.
### Geographic situation and access to crossings
Mesenzana lies a short distance from the Ticino border. The main accesses to Ticino are via the Brogeda crossing, the main road linking the Varese Valley to Ticino, and the Gaggiolo crossing. The strategic location enables reaching the main Ticino economic poles in reasonable time, although exact travel times depend on the final destination in Ticino and traffic flow at the crossings — factors that condition the daily commuter’s planning.
Anyone living in Mesenzana and working in Ticino falls fully under the frontier worker regime. The implications are both administrative and fiscal: obligation to register with INPS, respecting the days of presence in Italy to maintain frontier worker status, and adherence to Italian declaration regimes. Moreover, it will be necessary to evaluate the health‑insurance option (Swiss LAMal or Italian SSN) and understand the pension implications (AVS, LPP, unemployment insurance).
### The New Frontier Workers Agreement and fiscal implications
The New Frontier Workers Agreement — signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified in Italy by Law 83 of 13 June 2023, entering into force on 1 January 2024 — introduced significant changes to the tax regime. New frontier workers, i.e. those who acquired this status from 17 July 2023 onwards, have a declarative allowance of €10'000 per year. Those who were already frontier workers before that date benefit from an exemption of €7'500, with a transitional regime foreseen until 2033.
This agreement represents an important evolution compared with the previous regime, as it simplifies certain declaration obligations and improves tax predictability for new commuters. However, anyone moving from Mesenzana to work in Ticino must understand the mechanism of the Italy‑Switzerland Convention against Double Taxation (signed 9 December 1976) and how the tax credit applicable in the CE section of the Italian 730 tax return recovers the taxes paid in Switzerland. ### Taxation and declaratory obligations
The tax system for those who reside in Mesenzana and work in Ticino follows precise rules. In Italy, the border worker is required to register with INPS as an employee and to file an annual tax return (Form 730 or Income Tax). However, the declared income is taxed exclusively in Switzerland, where the employer applies the tax at source. To avoid double taxation, Italy recognises a tax credit — indicated in the EC framework of declaration 730 — which allows taxes paid in Switzerland to be recovered.
The structure of the Swiss paycheck for a frontier worker includes deductions for:
- **AVS/AI/IPG** (old-age and disability insurance): 5.3% to be paid by the employee - Unemployment (AD) and accident (AC) insurance: 1.1% up to CHF 148'200 of income - LAINF (accident insurance): 0.7–1.5% - LPP (pension fund according to pillar): 7–18% depending on the age group (from 25 years) - Cantonal/municipal source tax: withheld as a percentage of gross income
In Italy, on the other hand, the border worker pays:
- INPS (social security contributions): percentage calculated by the Swiss employer on a bilateral basis - IRPEF (Personal Income Tax): progressive rates from 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% over €50,000
### Sickness insurance and social security
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for those who
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Pre-transfer Checklist
Before moving to Mesenzana and starting a frontier worker activity in Ticino, it is advisable to check some key points:
1. **Employment Contract**: Ensure that the Swiss employer is willing to offer a frontier worker contract with the appropriate deductions and communications to INPS.
2. Frontier Worker Permit (Permit G): Request the permit from the competent local Italian authority (municipality of Mesenzana) in coordination with the Swiss SEM (State Secretariat for Migration). The procedure varies depending on the destination canton for work.
3. Registration with INPS: Once hired, register with INPS as a frontier worker employee. The Swiss employer will submit contribution data in a bilateral scheme.
4. LAMal or SSN Choice: Decide within the established deadlines whether to keep Italian health insurance (free SSN) or switch to Swiss LAMal (with monthly premium).
5. Tax and Accounting Tracking: Prepare a system to keep Swiss pay slips, Italian tax declarations, and expense invoices (especially if you intend to seek deductions for commuting costs — although their deductibility depends on the applicable Italian regime).
6. Residence and Notifications: Register your change of residence at the Mesenzana municipality and notify INPS within 30 days.
### Tools and Available Resources
Our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to estimate your monthly net income considering Italian (INPS) and Swiss deductions (AVS, LPP, LAMal, source tax). By entering your Swiss gross salary, you can see the impact of both tax systems and plan a realistic monthly budget.
For an in-depth analysis of double taxation effects and available tax refunds, see our guide on [tax refunds](nav:ristorni). Additionally, the [cost of living comparison](nav:cost-of-living) tool for Ticino-Italy will help you quantify the actual economic advantage of moving to Mesenzana.
Before purchasing health insurance, consult our page on [LAMal and health insurance](nav:health) to compare options between Swiss LAMal and Italian SSN based on your family situation. Use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your monthly net income considering the LAMal-SSN choice and plan your move with complete tax awareness.

item.title: The book about the border worker boom in Switzerland
item.description: New academic book explains how Switzerland has 400,000 frontier workers. From 84,000 in 1978 to the boom after 2000. Focus on wages, taxation, transport.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Switzerland with 400,000+ cross-border workers: first European country by number - An academic book explains the boom: from 84,000 in 1978 to today - Three areas absorb 80%: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino, Basel cantons - Topics addressed: wages, taxation, transport, xenophobia, social security
## Key facts - **What**: Publication of the book 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse – 30 questions' (Alphil) - When: Recent release; acceleration since 2000 (EU-CH free movement agreement) - Where: Switzerland; focus on 3 geographical areas (80% of cross-border workforce) - Who: Authors: Stéphane Rossini, Jean-Claude Rennwald, Daniel Droz, Alexandre Moine - Number: 400,000 cross-border workers today vs 84,000 in 1978 (5x growth in ~50 years)
### The cross-border worker boom in numbers
Switzerland has become the European country employing the largest number of cross-border workers. In 1978, following the 1974-75 economic crisis, there were 84,000. Today, they exceed 400,000. This jump was not linear, but underwent a decisive acceleration after 2000, the year the agreement on the free movement of persons between Switzerland and the European Union came into force — also favored by the robustness of the Swiss economy.
A new book, titled 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse – 30 questions' and published by Alphil editions, aims to clarify a continuously growing phenomenon: debunking myths and analyzing challenges and opportunities through statistical data and answers to key questions. In public debate, the phenomenon of cross-border workers is often at the center of controversy and misunderstanding.
### The authors and academic expertise
The book is authored by four experts of international standing: Stéphane Rossini (former Socialist National Councilor from Valais, former director of the Federal Social Insurance Office), Jean-Claude Rennwald (former National Councilor from Jura and trade unionist), Daniel Droz (journalist from Arcinfo), and Alexandre Moine (geographer). This combination of political, union, journalistic, and geographical expertise allows for a 360-degree analysis of the phenomenon.
The work focuses on the three geographical areas that alone absorb over 80% of the cross-border workforce: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino, and the two cantons of Basel. In these regions, cross-border work is structural to the local economy and the relationship with neighboring countries. The themes covered in the volume range from economic aspects to social and infrastructural issues: employment, wages, social dumping, social security, taxation, vocational training, housing availability, spatial planning, transport, teleworking, and the delicate relationship between cross-border workers and resident workers, as well as between states and European authorities. ### The three key areas: geographical concentration and reasons
The concentration of border workers in three specific areas — French Switzerland, Ticino, Basel — is no coincidence. These regions benefit from geographical proximity to neighbouring countries, a robust local economy, and a historical tradition of cross-border economic exchanges. Ticino, in particular, serves as a bridge to the Italian Lombard economy. French Switzerland overlooks France, while Basel borders France and Germany.
This geographical concentration creates challenges common to all three areas: infrastructural pressure on border crossings, traffic congestion, coordination needs between health and social security systems, and local debates on competition in labour markets.
### Contemporary challenges: from social dumping to xenophobia
The book addresses issues crucial to the daily life of the border worker. A first area concerns wages and social dumping: are frontier workers really paid less than resident workers? To what extent does their inflow affect local Swiss wages?
Social security is another priority. How does health insurance, the AVS (old-age pension) and the second pillar (LPP) work for those who work in Switzerland but reside in Italy? These issues directly affect the protection of the border worker during their working life.
Traffic is a recurring theme in the public debate on border crossers. ### Dove trovare il libro e come approfondire
Il libro "Le travail frontalier en Suisse – 30 questions" è pubblicato dalle edizioni Alphil, un editore specializzato in scienze sociali e umanistiche con sede in Svizzera romanda. È possibile ordinarlo tramite i principali canali di vendita libraria online e presso le librerie specializzate in saggistica economica e sociale.
Per il frontaliere, questa pubblicazione rappresenta una risorsa preziosa per comprendere il contesto normativo, economico e sociale in cui opera. Leggerla significa acquisire una visione d'insieme delle sfide collettive — e non solo individuali — che caratterizzano il lavoro transfrontaliero. Non è soltanto una questione personale di busta paga o dichiarazione fiscale, ma di comprensione critica del fenomeno nel quale sei inserito.
### Approfondire i tuoi diritti: strumenti pratici
Accanto a questa lettura, è importante padroneggiare alcuni aspetti concreti della vita da frontaliere. Il tuo stipendio in Svizzera è calcolato secondo regole specifiche, così come i contributi sociali (AVS, secondo pilastro LPP, assicurazione malattia). Le tasse e gli ristorni seguono convenzioni bilaterali tra Svizzera e Italia.
Puoi verificare in autonomia come il tuo reddito lordo si trasforma in netto utilizzando il [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) del nostro sito. Questo strumento ti aiuta a capire l'impatto reale di contributi e imposte sulla tua busta paga, mese dopo mese.
Se cerchi un nuovo lavoro oltre confine o desideri monitorare le opportunità nel mercato frontaliero, gli [annunci di lavoro](nav:jobs) specializzati in questo segmento raccolgono proposte da aziende ticinesi e svizzere che assumono attivamente frontalieri.
### Protezione dalla disoccupazione e gestione fiscale
Un altro aspetto affrontato dal libro è il rapporto tra frontalieri e precarietà occupazionale. Se il tuo contratto venisse risolto, come funziona l'assicurazione contro la disoccupazione? Quali diritti hai? Per comprendere meglio questo tema, consulta la sezione dedicata alla [disoccupazione per frontalieri](nav:unemployment) sul nostro sito.
Altrettanto cruciale è la [dichiarazione dei redditi](nav:tax-return): un passaggio obbligatorio annuale che richiede attenzione ai dettagli per versamenti, ritenute e crediti d'imposta. Una guida specializzata può fare la differenza nella gestione corretta della tua posizione fiscale. Non lasciare il tuo futuro finanziario al caso. Accedi oggi stesso al [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) e verifica quanto stai effettivamente guadagnando dopo tutti i prelievi.

item.description: Railway line interrupted until Wednesday 9 September 2026 at 4:00 am. Replacement buses available but with guaranteed delays and no connections.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- S30 line completely blocked between Cadenazzo and Luino due to technical failure of the railway system - Extended interruption until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM - Replacement buses in service with no guarantee of connections - Cross-border workers advised to check information before departure and add 30-45 minutes to travel time
## Key facts
- **What**: Complete interruption of railway traffic on the S30 line - Where: Route Cadenazzo (Ticino) – Luino (Italy, Lombardy) - When: Until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM - Cause: Technical failure of the railway system - Temporary solution: Replacement buses with possible delays
---
Railway traffic on the S30 line between Cadenazzo and Luino is completely interrupted. A technical failure of the railway system has made it impossible for trains to circulate on the cross-border route. The interruption will continue at least until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM, directly affecting cross-border workers who depend on this connection to reach their workplace in Lombardy.
To ensure a minimum connection between Ticino and Italy, replacement bus services have been arranged. However, the situation remains complicated: passengers have been explicitly advised to account for significant waiting times and possible delays. A particularly important warning: connections cannot be guaranteed. This means that those relying on coordinated transfers between different means of transport could find themselves stranded for long periods at stations.
### The impact on cross-border mobility
For cross-border workers who daily cross the border for work purposes, the loss of the S30 line is not a simple inconvenience. It is a disruption to routine. Those who regularly use the train have structured their schedules around railway punctuality: departure at 6:45 AM, arrival at 7:30 AM, shift start at 8:00 AM. With replacement buses, the same journey could take 75-90 minutes, making it impossible to maintain usual schedules. Anyone traveling between Ticino and Luino must check information shortly before departure and plan for extra travel time — these are not theoretical suggestions, but a concrete necessity to avoid risking being late at work. ## How the service disruption affects cross-border commuters
The S30 line disruption directly impacts those who have built a mobility routine on this route. For many cross-border commuters, deciding how to travel over the next two days is not straightforward. The replacement bus is available, but requires rigid planning: waiting times at stops are predictable, but bus schedules do not perfectly align with the train schedules they are meant to replace. Those accustomed to reading the newspaper during their train commute will instead need to find a seat on a potentially crowded bus.
The psychological aspect is also at stake: the bus is slower, exposes commuters to road traffic, introduces variability. A 24-30 hour railway interruption generates stress among cross-border commuters, especially if they have no plan B. Those who have access to a private car might consider driving through border crossings, but this introduces additional fuel costs. Those entirely dependent on public transport have no choice but to adapt to the replacement buses and accept the inevitable delays.
### What changes in daily travel management
The official recommendation to 'inform yourself shortly before departure' is not a mere suggestion. It means contacting railway operators, consulting mobility apps (SBB Mobil, Trenord), checking for updates on delays or cancellations. A positive development in repairs could accelerate restoration; a negative development could prolong the interruption. Between 30-60 minutes before departure, it is essential to have the most current information, because the situation can change rapidly.
For employers who hire cross-border commuters, this period represents a management challenge: documented delays cannot be charged to workers, but still create organizational problems. For cross-border commuters themselves, the risk is concrete: one or two days of small delays could go unnoticed, but the message sent to the employer (even if unfair) is unreliability. The psychological pressure is real.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## How to Organize During the Interruption
If you regularly travel on the Cadenazzo–Luino route for work, consider these concrete steps in the coming two days:
**Contact your employer**: Report the railway service interruption before the morning. Many employers, especially in Lombardy, understand cross-border service disruptions and can allow a delayed departure or authorize exceptional remote work for that day.
Check official bus schedules: SBB Mobil, Trenord and local bus operators will provide updated schedules. Don't rely on third-hand information or social media. Official apps are the source of truth.
Add buffer time: If your normal journey takes 45 minutes by train, expect 90 minutes by bus. Leave 30-45 minutes earlier than you normally would. This safety margin protects you from surprises.
Consider alternative transport: If you have access to a private car and fuel costs are manageable, consider a private ride or carpooling with other cross-border workers in the same situation. Ask in Ticino cross-border worker WhatsApp groups if anyone is organizing a ride to the Luino area.
### Timeline and Deadlines
The interruption continues until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 4:00 AM. This means that Tuesday, September 8 (today) the service is blocked, and will remain so for the entire day and the following night. Starting at 4:00 AM on Wednesday morning, normal railway traffic on the route is expected to resume. If you work night shifts or are returning very late Tuesday evening, check if there are replacement buses in the evening hours as well, since some routes may be reduced or cancelled during the night.
### Resources and Support Links
To organize yourself best, consult the [border crossing guide](nav:border) if you are considering road alternatives, and learn how to plan the costs of your daily commute as a cross-border worker. Stay updated by frequently checking official channels until complete restoration. Share reliable information with fellow cross-border workers — the informal support network is precious in these critical moments.
First day as a cross-border worker? Our [practical guide](nav:first-day) walks you from cantonal registration to your first paycheck.

item.title: Swiss cross-border commuters: 400,000, myths and analysis
item.description: Switzerland employs 400,000+ border workers (European record). New book dispels myths: growth 1978–2026, wages, taxation, transport. Ticino in the centre.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Switzerland employs 400,000+ cross-border workers: European record in 2026 - From 1978 to today: growth from 84,000 to over 400,000 (+376%) - New book analyzes myths, salaries, taxation and cross-border transport - Ticino, French-speaking Switzerland and Basel absorb 80% of the workforce
## Key Facts - **What**: Book 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse - 30 questions' debunks myths and analyzes the phenomenon - When: Published in 2026 (data from 1978 to today) - Where: Three main areas: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino, Basel - Who: Authors: Stéphane Rossini (former director of FSIO), Jean-Claude Rennwald (former union leader), Daniel Droz (journalist), Alexandre Moine (geographer) - Amount: 84,000 cross-border workers in 1978 → 400,000+ in 2026 - Publisher: Alphil - Agreement: Free movement Switzerland-EU since 2000
Switzerland has achieved an unprecedented milestone in Europe: it employs over 400,000 cross-border workers. To understand what this means in concrete terms, one need only look at the past. In 1978, following the economic crisis of 1974-75, there were only 84,000 cross-border workers. The leap in time — from just under 100,000 to four times as many — was not linear, but experienced a decisive acceleration after 2000, when the agreement on the free movement of persons between Switzerland and the European Union came into force. The robustness of the Swiss economy did the rest.
A new book titled 'Le travail frontalier en Suisse - 30 questions' (Alphil) addresses this reality with data in hand. The authors are four: the former socialist national councillors Stéphane Rossini (Valais, former director of the Federal Office of Social Insurance) and Jean-Claude Rennwald (Jura, union leader), supported by journalist Daniel Droz and geographer Alexandre Moine. The work focuses on three geographic areas that alone absorb over 80% of the cross-border workforce: French-speaking Switzerland, Ticino and the two cantons of Basel.
### From Numbers to Myths
The themes addressed by the book are multiple: employment, wages, social dumping, social security, taxation, training, housing, territorial planning and transport. But there is a question that recurs frequently in public debates: do cross-border workers really steal jobs from resident workers? For Rennwald, xenophobic reflexes towards cross-border workers seem less pronounced today compared to a few decades ago. They could, however, ease further if the use of public transport were to increase. Traffic on roads and highways, with its eternal congestion, remains indeed one of the main sources of friction between communities. ### Structural growth in 48 years
From 1978 to 2026, the number of cross-border workers in Switzerland has grown nearly 4.8 times. It is not a random growth, nor is it a consequence of massive immigration. Rather, it is the structural result of two factors: the economic integration that followed the free movement agreement of 2000, and the persistent development disparity between European economies. Switzerland, with its salaries and the quality of work, remains a powerful pole of attraction for those living on the other side of the border — especially in Ticino, where the borders with Italy allow a daily commute that is not always easy, but feasible.
The three areas that absorb over 80% of the cross-border workforce have diverse characteristics. French-speaking Switzerland (Vaud, Jura, Valais, Geneva) attracts mainly from border regions in France. Ticino, especially with the Mendrisio district, engages with Lombard provinces. The two Basel cantons (BS and BL) receive workers from Alsace, central France, and southwestern Germany. Each area has developed a cross-border economy with its own peculiarities and specific labor market dynamics.
### The myth of the 'theft of jobs'
The question of whether cross-border workers 'steal jobs from residents' is complex. The book does not provide a simplistic answer. According to the authors, cross-border work is the result of globalization and unequal development in the capitalist system. For this reason, say Rossini and Rennwald, it will be possible to regulate it only through the construction of a social Switzerland and a social Europe — that is, through greater harmonization of salaries, labor rights, and social protection between countries.
Wage dumping, differentiated taxation, and the lack of equal protections remain critical points. However, the authors note that xenophobic reactions toward cross-border workers are today less pronounced than they were a few decades ago. One of the causes of this change is the growing acceptance that the phenomenon is not reversible — it is a structural characteristic of contemporary Europe, not a temporary exception.
### The role of transportation in public opinion
An interesting discovery from the book: traffic and congestion at Alpine passes remain one of the strongest sources of friction between Swiss residents and cross-border workers. It is not directly a matter of employment, but of daily livability. The more cross-border workers use public transport — buses, trains, organized shuttles — the less visibility congestion at highways has. Paradoxically, better public transportation infrastructure could reduce tensions more than any awareness campaign, making commuting less perceptible to the local community.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What it means concretely for the cross-border worker
If you work daily across the border, the content of this book concerns you directly. It is not an abstract treatise on economic sociology, but a manual that answers 30 concrete questions about the aspects that affect your life: salaries, taxes, permits, social security, housing and mobility.
The growth from 84,000 to 400,000 cross-border workers in 48 years means that your status is no longer considered an anomaly, but a permanent reality of the Swiss economy. This has positive implications (greater regulatory recognition, more stable bilateral agreements) and persistent challenges (wage competition in low-skilled sectors, fiscal complexity in double taxation). The book analyzes how these phenomena manifest in the three main areas — including Ticino — and what role public policies play in regulating them.
### Where to deepen and which tools to use
For those wishing to read the complete book, «Le travail frontalier en Suisse - 30 questions» is available from the publisher Alphil and in major Swiss bookstores. If instead you are interested in understanding the specific fiscal and salary impacts of your situation, the Frontaliere Ticino website provides [a net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and [tax return tools](nav:tax-return) that allow you to concretely see how the various components of your income are composed month by month.
Furthermore, if you wish to explore additional [job offers in Switzerland](nav:jobs) in light of these analyses, you can consult the dedicated section. The book provides the general framework; our tools help you navigate daily practice, transforming theory into real numbers of your payslip.
### Final point: European regulation and social protection
The authors are clear on one point: cross-border work will not decrease. It will continue to grow as long as economic disparities between neighboring countries persist. The only realistic path is to increase social protection standards, minimum wages and labour rights in a coordinated manner between Switzerland and the EU. This may seem a distant vision, but it is a truth that the book's historical research documents: the phenomenon is too large to be addressed with restrictive measures. It must instead be regulated, protected, made transparent and fair. If you are a cross-border worker, this book offers you the context to understand how public policies affect you — and why your voice in public debate matters.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/svizzera/attualita/1948807/svizzera-frontalieri-lavoro-europa-residenti-rubano)*
